name: Crop Water Requirement Calculator (ETc)
seoTitle: Crop Water Requirement (ETc) Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: A crop's water use is the reference evapotranspiration multiplied by a crop coefficient: ETc = Kc × ETo. Free crop water requirement (etc) calculator: enter y
summary:
A crop's water use is the reference evapotranspiration multiplied by a crop coefficient: ETc = Kc × ETo. It returns crop water use, seasonal use (120 days), volume to apply per hectare and hours a 10 m³/h system must run, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator gives daily and seasonal water use per hectare, the irrigation volume and how long a system must run to deliver it. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Crop Water Requirement (ETc)
sections.html:
ETc = Kc × ETo; volume (m³/ha) = ETc (mm) × 10 ÷ efficiency

sections.title: How do I use the Crop Water Requirement (ETc)?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: reference evapotranspiration (eto) of 5.4 mm/day, crop coefficient (kc) of 1.05, area of 1 ha, irrigation efficiency of 80%.

Substituting them into the formula gives crop water use of 5.67 mm/day, seasonal use (120 days) of 680.4 mm, volume to apply per hectare of 70.88 m³/ha/day, hours a 10 m³/h system must run of 7.09 h.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• One millimetre over one hectare is 10 m³ of water — the conversion that makes irrigation arithmetic easy.

  • Kc changes through the season: about 0.3 at emergence, 1.0–1.2 at mid-season, and falling as the crop senesces.

  • Irrigation efficiency divides the requirement: 80% efficiency means a fifth of the water never reaches the root zone.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Using a single Kc for the whole season.
  • Treating mm as litres per square metre — they are numerically equal, which is a help, not a licence to mix the units.
  • Ignoring rainfall, which reduces the irrigation requirement.

faq.q: How much water is 5 mm/day per hectare?
What does the Crop Water Requirement (ETc) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns crop water use, seasonal use (120 days), volume to apply per hectare and hours a 10 m³/h system must run. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
